   - `WEAVE_DISABLED=true` disables tracing for the whole program. It is read only once, at function-definition time, so it can't be toggled at runtime [S2].

2. **Did you initialize Weave and instrument the code?**
   - Call `weave.init('your-team/project_name')`. If you don't set a team, traces go to your default team. If the project doesn't exist, Weave creates it. So the traces may be in a different team or project than the one you're viewing [S1].
   - Weave tracks calls to supported LLMs automatically. To track your own functions, add `@weave.op()` in Python or `weave.op(fn)` in TypeScript [S1].
   - In the quickstart, calling a traced function prints links in the terminal for viewing your traces [S1]. You can compare your own run's output with that.

   - `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. Agent traces appear on the **Agents** page. They are separate, even within the same project [S3].

sources.heading: Environment variable
sources.text:
## Environment variable

Use an environment variable when you want to disable tracing for the entire program without modifying application code.

To unconditionally disable tracing for the entire program, set the environment variable `WEAVE_DISABLED=true`.

`WEAVE_DISABLED` is read only once, at function-definition time. You can't use this variable to toggle tracing at runtime.

sources.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

# What is Weave?

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

# TypeScript SDK: third-party integration guide

> Integrate third-party libraries with the Weave TypeScript SDK

This guide describes how to integrate third-party libraries (for example, OpenAI) with the Weave TypeScript SDK. It's intended for TypeScript developers who want Weave to automatically trace calls to supported libraries in their application.

Weave supports automatic instrumentation, which streamlines setup and reduces the need for manual configuration.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **What changed?**
> As of [PR #4554](https://github.com/wandb/weave/pull/4554), Weave automatically patches supported libraries such as OpenAI when it loads. You no longer need to manually wrap them:
>
> ```ts twoslash lines theme={"system"}
> // @noErrors
> weave.wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI());
> ```
>
> Weave handles this automatically in most cases. However, [edge cases](#advanced-usage) may occur.

### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

## Environment variable

Use an environment variable when you want to disable tracing for the entire program without modifying application code.

To unconditionally disable tracing for the entire program, set the environment variable `WEAVE_DISABLED=true`.

`WEAVE_DISABLED` is read only once, at function-definition time. You can't use this variable to toggle tracing at runtime.

sources.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

## View projects in the UI

To access a project in the Weights & Biases UI:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb).
2. Select the **Weights & Biases logo** in the upper-left corner to open the **Global navigation menu**, then select your project from the **Projects** sidebar. This opens the project's overview page, or the **Traces** page if you've already logged traces to the project.
3. From the overview page, you can:
   * Review your project's statistics, such as the number of traces logged to the project and how much storage the project uses.

   - `WEAVE_DISABLED=true` disables tracing for the whole program. It is read only once, at function-definition time, so it can't be toggled at runtime [S2].

   - Weave tracks calls to supported LLMs automatically. To track your own functions, add `@weave.op()` in Python or `weave.op(fn)` in TypeScript [S1].
